newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger warns "socialists" would hurt economy.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger warns "socialists" would hurt economy.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger accused Labour leader Helen Clark on Thursday of teaming up with old-style socialists who would turn back the clock and damage the economy.
Bolger, fighting a rearguard action just two days before a general election, portrayed Clark as hostage to the high-tax, high-spending Alliance in any government of the left.

"The concerns about a return to yesteryear under a Labour-led left-wing coalition have increased in my view as the campaign has gone on, and could be influential in the final vote on Saturday," he said.
Clark countered with accusations of scaremongering and hypocrisy as she battled to keep her campaign initiative and end six years of conservative government.
The latest polls show Labour closing to within a few points of Bolger's National Party in the run-up to New Zealand's first election under proportional representation.
Both would need coalition partners to govern, but the polls show that Labour, nationalist New Zealand First and the left-wing Alliance look set to win a majority of seats.
Bolger, campaigning on his government's record of strong economic growth, renewed warnings that a Labour-led government would take the country backwards.
In a televised debate, he cited a recent survey showing company bosses overwhelmingly favoured his economic stewardship over Clark's.
"There are people who believe in the old socialist philosophies, and Helen's joining them again," he said in reference to the Alliance and its leader Jim Anderton.
"There is a difference (of view) from the commercial world as to whether Helen Clark actually can run the economy. She can't. She'll join Jim Anderton."
Financial markets distrust Alliance policies, including higher import tariffs and a tax on all bank transactions, but are broadly comfortable with Labour's plans.
"I've been disappointed that Mr Bolger has fed a lot of scaremongering and rumouring about the New Zealand economy. I know it can be sound and positive and deliver for our people," Clark said.
Labour hopes to strike a coalition deal with New Zealand First and win Alliance support on social policy, health and education initiatives.
National must pin its hopes on radical free-market Act New Zealand, which looks increasingly confident of clearing the five percent threshold of votes required to enter parliament.
The wild card is New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, who again refused on Thursday to say whether he would take his party into coalition with Labour or National.

Political commentators say there is too much bad blood between Peters and Bolger, who sacked him as a National cabinet minister in 1991, and opinion polls suggest New Zealand First supporters would much prefer a coalition with Labour.
